summary: Describes a set of mappings between X.400 mail systems and systems using the RFC 822 mail format. X.400 was a CCITT standard for store-and-forward messaging, and these mappings let the two worlds interwork. It was a proposed protocol, was updated by RFC 1026, RFC 1138 and RFC 1148, and was replaced by RFC 1327 and RFC 2156.

plainLanguage.summary:
Two communities used different mail standards. This RFC is the rulebook that lets a gateway, a program that sits between them, translate a message from one into the other without losing what it says.

It covers the addresses, the message layers and the individual services, such as delivery reports, that a gateway has to reproduce on the other side.

subtitle: The rules a mail gateway follows to translate messages between X.400 systems and RFC 822 Internet mail.

tldr.problem: Large communities used RFC 822 mail while X.400 was expected to be widely implemented, and the two systems use different address formats, different message layers and different service elements.
tldr.mechanism: A gateway maps X.400 addresses and protocol elements onto RFC 822 addresses and header fields and back, using a defined textual form for X.400 addresses, short escape codes for characters X.400 cannot carry, and new RFC 822 header fields for X.400 information.
tldr.outcome: RFC 987 was updated by RFC 1026, RFC 1138 and RFC 1148, and was obsoleted by RFC 1327 and RFC 2156.

today: RFC 987 has been obsoleted by RFC 1327 and RFC 2156, and updated by RFC 1026, RFC 1138 and RFC 1148. Those later RFCs are where the X.400 to RFC 822 mapping continued.

sections.title: Two Mail Systems and a Gateway
sections.content:
RFC 987 describes mappings that let systems running the CCITT X.400 (1984) protocols work with systems that use the RFC 822 mail format, or protocols derived from it. The aim is to offer as many services as possible across the boundary without making the mappings complicated, and without requiring any change to the end systems themselves.

RFC 822 mail grew up on the ARPA-Internet together with SMTP (RFC 821) and a domain name system (RFC 920). RFC 822, or protocols derived from it, were also used on UUCP networks, on CSNET, on BITNET and on the JNT Mail networks, and the mappings here are said to suit all of them.

There were expected to be several gateways, sometimes called mail relays, and this specification exists so that they behave in the same way. Consistency matters most when a message passes through more than one gateway.

The guiding principles are stated up front. The specification should be pragmatic, with no complex mappings for academic reasons. Functionality across a gateway should be as high as possible. It is always a bad idea to lose information in a transformation, so a gateway should not discard information even when a requested service cannot be fully mapped. And a gateway has to understand the meaning of the objects it handles, not just their form, because it operates one layer above the layer it conceptually sits on.

The document has five chapters: the overview, the service elements, the basic mappings, addressing and protocol elements. Six appendices cover quoted string encodings, the mappings specific to JNT Mail, Internet mail, Phonenet mail and UUCP mail, and the format of the address mapping tables.
sections.plainLanguage: Two communities used different mail standards. This RFC is the rulebook that lets a gateway, a program that sits between them, translate a message from one into the other without losing what it says.

sections.title: How a Message Crosses the Gateway
sections.content:
X.400 is built in layers. The Message Transfer Service, provided by the P1 or P3 protocol, passes messages between Message Transfer Agents (MTAs) as a file format called a Message Protocol Data Unit (MPDU). There are three kinds: a User MPDU carrying an envelope and uninterpreted contents, a Probe carrying only an envelope, used to ask whether a message could be delivered to a given originator/recipient name, and a Delivery Report carrying an envelope and the result of a delivery attempt. Above that, the Interpersonal Messaging Service, provided by the P2 protocol, defines the Interpersonal Message with a heading and a body of body parts, and a Status Report.

RFC 822 assumes an underlying service, called the 822-P1 service, that identifies a list of recipients, identifies an error return address, and transfers an RFC 822 message. An RFC 822 message is a header of fields followed by uninterpreted ASCII text.

The mapping cannot be a clean layer-on-layer match. Going from RFC 822 to X.400, an RFC 822 message and its 822-P1 information are always mapped into an Interpersonal Message and the associated P1 envelope. Going the other way, an RFC 822 message may be derived from a Delivery Report, from a Status Report and its envelope, or from an Interpersonal Message and its envelope. A Probe has to be serviced by the gateway itself, because RFC 822 has no equivalent. Any other User MPDU is not mapped and should be rejected at the gateway.
sections.plainLanguage: X.400 mail travels in two layers: an outer envelope that moves the message between mail servers, and an inner message with a heading and a body. RFC 822 mail has one layer. The gateway reads both sides of each message and writes the result out in the other form.

sections.title: Which Services Survive the Gateway
sections.content:
Chapter 2 goes through the end-user services of each system and states how far a gateway can support each one. A service counts as supported when it maps with the same meaning, loses no information, and any action it needs is carried out. Where a service maps only partly, the RFC says how much is supported.

Most RFC 822 header fields map straight across: Date:, From:, Sender:, Reply-To:, To:, Cc:, Bcc:, Message-Id:, In-Reply-To: for a single reference, References: and Subject:. Fields with no X.400 equivalent, such as Keywords:, Comments:, Encrypted:, the Resent-* fields and unknown fields like X-*, are passed in the message text, so the information still reaches the reader.

Going the other way, the RFC does not push X.400 elements into the body of an RFC 822 message. It defines new RFC 822 header fields for the converted indication, message identification, original encoded information types, disclosure of other recipients, grade of delivery, the auto-forwarded indication, the expiry date, importance, obsoleting and sensitivity, and says those fields are expected to be registered.

Some services cannot be provided at all. Receipt notification, non-receipt notification and body part encryption are not supported. A probe is serviced by the gateway, and a delivery notification is supported at the gateway.
sections.plainLanguage: Some parts of a message, such as who it is from and what it is about, translate directly. Parts with no counterpart in the other system are kept in the message text so that the reader still sees them.

sections.title: Basic Character and Value Encodings
sections.content:
The P1 and P2 protocols are encoded in a structured binary form defined by X.409, while RFC 822 is text. Chapter 3 therefore defines how X.400 values are written as text. A gateway treats IA5 as ASCII, so the two are handled identically.

Booleans become TRUE or FALSE, and numeric strings become digits. A PrintableString is a restricted set of IA5 characters, and it leaves out several characters that are common in mail addresses. The RFC defines escapes for them: (a) for the at sign, (p) for the percent sign, (b) for the exclamation mark, (q) for the double quote and (u) for the underscore. Any other ASCII character is written as an opening parenthesis, three decimal digits and a closing parenthesis, with the digits running from 0 to 127. The mapping is deliberately asymmetric, and the RFC says it does not try to minimise the number of awkward cases.

Timestamps map symmetrically between UTCTime and the RFC 822 date-time syntax, and the UTCTime form that carries the time zone offset should be used. T.61 strings, which carry text meant for people to read, follow the CEN/CENELEC mappings from X.408.
sections.plainLanguage: Some symbols are not allowed in the X.400 character set, so the gateway writes them with short codes. The at sign becomes (a), for example, and any other character can be written as three digits in parentheses.

sections.title: Mapping Addresses Between the Two Systems
sections.content:
The RFC calls addressing probably the hardest part of the gateway and gives it a chapter of its own. An X.400 address is an O/R name: a set of attribute and value pairs such as country (C), administration domain (ADMD), private domain (PRMD), organisation (O), organisational unit (OU) and the parts of a personal name. The chapter also defines a standard textual form for it, a sequence of /attribute=value/ pairs, and a shorter personal name form such as Marshall.Rose or M.T.Rose.

The mapping is asymmetric, for two reasons. The two syntaxes are too different to match cleanly, and in general there would not be the administrative cooperation between the X.400 and RFC 822 worlds that a symmetric mapping would need.

Going from X.400 to RFC 822, the O/R name is written into the local part of the RFC 822 address, and the domain can supply some of the attributes. A table links domains to attributes: the domain AC.UK might imply a country, an ADMD and a PRMD, and the domain R-D.Salford.AC.UK would then add the organisation and organisational unit. Going the other way, a genuine RFC 822 address is carried inside the X.400 address as a domain defined attribute of type RFC-822, JNT-Mail or UUCP, depending on the world it should be read in.

The mapping from RFC 822 to X.400 runs in two stages. The gateway first tries to read the address as an X.400 encoding: it looks the domain up in its table of known domains, maps the local part to ASCII and parses the result as an O/R name. If that fails, the address is treated as a genuine RFC 822 address. A genuine RFC 822 recipient address has to be rejected, because X.400 needs to interpret it, but the return address and any addresses in the header are carried inside the domain defined attribute instead.
sections.plainLanguage: An X.400 address is a list of labelled parts, such as country, company and personal name. An Internet address is a name at a place. The gateway turns the first kind into the second, and when it cannot, it carries the Internet address inside one labelled part of the X.400 address.

sections.title: Mapping Messages, Probes and Reports
sections.content:
Chapter 5 gives the field-by-field mappings. Going from RFC 822 to X.400, the header fields build both the P1 envelope and the P2 heading, and the message body becomes an IA5 text body part. If any header fields have no X.400 equivalent, the message gets a first body part that starts with the line RFC-822-Headers: and holds those fields in their original order.

The RFC also defines new RFC 822 fields that carry X.400 information: P1-Message-ID, X400-Trace, Original-Encoded-Information-Types, P1-Content-Type, UA-Content-ID, Priority, P1-Recipient, Deferred-Delivery, Bilateral-Info, Obsoletes, Expiry-Date, Reply-By, Importance, Sensitivity and Autoforwarded. Delivery reports add a further set, such as Delivery-Report-Content-Original and Delivery-Report-Content-Reported-Recipient-Info.

Going from X.400 to RFC 822, the gateway builds a pro-forma message and fills it in from the X.400 elements. A probe is answered by the gateway itself. A delivery report becomes an RFC 822 message from an administrator at the gateway, with the body giving a readable description of the failure and, where possible, the original message.

Return of contents is handled in one of two ways. Where X.400 systems support it widely, the gateway asks for a confirmed report and passes the result straight back. Where it is not widely supported, the gateway keeps track itself: it notes each delivery report, and if no report comes back for a recipient it sends a timeout failure notice to the RFC 822 originator.
sections.plainLanguage: Each part of a message goes into the matching slot of the other system. Parts with no slot go into a note at the top of the message, so the reader still sees them. Delivery failures come back as ordinary mail messages from the gateway.
